intro: Five of Bristol's remarkable trees stand on one walk of about two kilometres through the centre: the planes of Queen Square, a fig growing out of the harbour wall by Bristol Bridge, the city's largest black mulberry in Royal Fort Gardens, the oldest oak on Brandon Hill and a cedar 5.95 metres round in Clifton's Victoria Square. The oldest stand further out, in parkland estates the city inherited from merchant families: Ashton Court's Domesday Oak, around 700 years old, a Repton-era cedar at Blaise Castle and an oak older than Vanbrugh's house at Kings Weston. Twelve trees in all.
meta_description: Twelve remarkable trees in Bristol: a central walk from Queen Square's planes to a Clifton cedar, plus Ashton Court's 700-year-old Domesday Oak.
question_answer: Bristol's oldest tree is the Domesday Oak in Ashton Court Estate, estimated at around 700 years old and named for the estate's mention in the 1086 Domesday Book. Its trunk has partially collapsed and is now held together with timber struts and wire, but it is still alive, one of Britain's 50 Great Trees named by the Tree Council in 2002. It stands free to visit in Ashton Court, a short bus ride from central Bristol.
question_meta: The Domesday Oak in Ashton Court, around 700 years old, is Bristol's oldest tree, still alive despite a partly collapsed, wire-supported trunk.
question_context: Ashton Court was a private deer park for centuries before Bristol City Council bought it in 1959 and opened it to the public. Its oldest surviving oak, thought to be around 700 years old, takes its name from the estate's own appearance in the Domesday Book of 1086; the Tree Council believes the tree was already growing around the time that record was made. In 2002, to mark the Queen's golden jubilee, the Tree Council selected it as one of 50 Great British Trees. Its trunk has since partially collapsed, split and settled toward the ground, and is now held upright with timber struts and steel wire. It is thinner in the canopy than it was, but still comes into leaf each year. It stands, easy to miss without signage, among Ashton Court's wider population of ancient pollard oaks, more than a hundred of them, the largest such cluster in Britain outside Windsor Great Park. In the city centre, the oldest tree on record is the oak on Brandon Hill, which the Bristol Tree Forum estimates at around 300 years, five metres round, standing just inside the park keepers' compound.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Bristol?
faq.a: The Domesday Oak in Ashton Court, around 700 years old and named for the estate's mention in the 1086 Domesday Book. Its trunk has partly collapsed and is held up with struts and wire, but it is still alive.

faq.q: Where can I see old trees in central Bristol?
faq.a: On foot in an afternoon. Start at the London Planes of Queen Square, then the fig growing out of the harbour wall east of Bristol Bridge, the city's largest black mulberry in Royal Fort Gardens, the oak on Brandon Hill and the cedar in Victoria Square, Clifton, about two kilometres in all and free throughout.

faq.q: Is Ashton Court free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. Ashton Court Estate is owned and managed by Bristol City Council and is open daily from 8am at no charge, though a small car parking fee applies for drivers.

faq.q: What trees are at Blaise Castle Estate?
faq.a: Cedars of Lebanon, an Atlas cedar, a Wellingtonia and a holm oak stand among the specimen trees the landscape designer Humphry Repton planted for the estate in the late 1790s. The grounds have been a free public park since 1926.

faq.q: How old are the trees in Queen Square, Bristol?
faq.a: The London Planes around Queen Square's edge date to roughly the 1880s, making them around 145 years old. They replaced earlier avenue plantings from 1716, part of a square that has stood since 1699.

trees.name: The Domesday Oak

location.address: Ashton Court Estate, Long Ashton, Bristol BS41 9JN

trees.story: Ashton Court appears in the Domesday Book, the survey William the Conqueror ordered of his new kingdom in 1086, and one oak in the estate's parkland is thought to have already been growing around that time, which is where its name comes from. At an estimated 700 years old, it may be the oldest living tree in greater Bristol. Its condition tells the story as plainly as its age: the trunk has split and partially collapsed, one section settling almost horizontally toward the ground while the rest hangs on, now held upright by timber struts and steel wire rather than its own strength. Visitors who knew the tree decades ago recall climbing inside a fuller, healthier trunk; today's crown is thinner and the bark flaking with decay. In 2002, the Tree Council named it one of 50 Great British Trees to mark the Queen's golden jubilee, official recognition for a specimen that has no sign or marker pointing casual visitors to it today, easy to walk past in a park that holds more than a hundred other ancient pollard oaks, the largest such cluster in Britain outside Windsor Great Park.

best_time.label: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.access: Free, open access, Ashton Court Estate (daily from 8am, closing time varies by season)
trees.transport: Bus or short drive from central Bristol; no on-site rail
trees.notes: Corroborated by the Ancient Tree Forum's dedicated site page and a Bristol247 feature article, both independently describing the tree's condition (partial collapse, struts and wire support), its 700-year age estimate, the Domesday Book naming story, and the 2002 Tree Council 'Great British Tree' designation. Cross-checked against a 2017 social media post from a local heritage account describing the same collapse and support structure, consistent across multiple years. Genuinely alive as of the most recent (2025) source checked this run, though in decline. Coordinates are Ashton Court Estate's general point (Nominatim-geocoded), not a surveyed position for this specific tree within the large estate; visitor reports note it lacks on-site signage and can be hard to find, reinforcing that no precise public coordinate exists yet.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the props: the trunk has split, one section settling almost horizontally, and what is left is held up by timber struts and steel wire. It stands unsigned in Ashton Court's parkland of pollard oaks.

trees.name: The Sweet Chestnut of Ashton Park

location.address: Ashton Court Estate, Long Ashton, Bristol BS41 9JN

trees.story: Sweet Chestnuts spiral as they age, their bark twisting around the trunk in a pattern that gets more pronounced with every passing century, and Ashton Park's oldest is a dramatic example: an estimated 600 years old, with a girth of over eight metres, according to the Bristol Tree Forum's own survey of the city's veteran trees. Sweet Chestnut is not native to Britain, introduced by the Romans and long favoured by estate owners for timber and for the nuts it produces, and a tree of this size and age likely dates to well before Ashton Court passed through its various private owners into Bristol City Council's hands in 1959. It shares its parkland with the Domesday Oak and more than a hundred other ancient pollard oaks, together forming the largest concentration of veteran trees anywhere in Britain outside Windsor Great Park, a legacy of centuries spent as private deer park rather than farmed or built over.
verified_sources: https://bristoltreeforum.org/meet-bristols-remarkable-trees/veteran-trees-in-the-public-realm/ (Bristol Tree Forum survey: Sweet Chestnut, Ashton Park, girth 805 cm, 'largest of a line of six')
trees.access: Free, open access, Ashton Court Estate (daily from 8am, closing time varies by season)

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon at Blaise Castle

location.address: Blaise Castle Estate, Kings Weston Road, Bristol BS10 7QS

trees.story: John Scandrett Harford, a wealthy Bristol banker, bought Blaise Castle Estate in 1789 and hired the two biggest names in English landscape design of the era, Humphry Repton and later John Nash, to remake it into a Picturesque parkland. Repton's method favoured framing views with carefully placed specimen trees rather than dense planting, and the Cedars of Lebanon he set out near Blaise Castle House are some of the estate's oldest surviving evidence of that design still growing where he placed it. Cedar of Lebanon was still a relatively novel import to English gardens at the time, prized for its wide, flat-tiered canopy and biblical associations, and a tree planted in Repton's era has now had well over two centuries to develop the broad, layered crown the species is known for. Bristol Corporation bought the estate in 1926, turning Harford's private grounds into a free public park, and the cedar has stood through that entire transition from private landscape statement to a tree thousands of Bristol families walk past on the way to the children's playground nearby.

best_time.label: upright barrel cones that sit on the branches like eggs

verified_sources: https://bristoltreeforum.org/meet-bristols-remarkable-trees/veteran-trees-in-the-public-realm/ (Bristol Tree Forum survey: Cedar of Lebanon at Blaise House close to the main house, girth 695 cm, 'the finest in Bristol')
trees.access: Free, open access, Blaise Castle Estate (daily, dawn to dusk)
trees.transport: Bus from central Bristol; no on-site rail
trees.notes: Girth (695cm) and age estimate (250 years) from the Bristol Tree Forum's veteran tree survey (grid reference ST5624 7869, 'Blaise House'); Bristol Museums' own history of the estate corroborates Repton and Nash's landscaping work for Harford from the 1790s and the 1926 sale to Bristol Corporation. No source gives an exact planting year for this specific cedar; age range reflects the Repton-era design period rather than a precise sourced date.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, broad and flat-tiered in layers the way a Cedar of Lebanon grows. It stands near Blaise Castle House where Repton placed it, close to the children's playground.

trees.name: The Oak of Kings Weston

location.address: Kings Weston Estate, Kings Weston Lane, Bristol BS11 0UR

trees.story: Sir John Vanbrugh, the architect behind Blenheim Palace and Castle Howard, designed Kings Weston House for the politician Edward Southwell between 1712 and 1719, one of the grandest early 18th-century houses in the Bristol area. An oak growing in the estate's parkland predates that whole building project by well over a century, already an old, established tree when Vanbrugh's workmen were still laying foundations. At an estimated 450 years, it is the oldest tree recorded on the entire estate, a living link to the land before Southwell's family ever owned it. Kings Weston's grounds also hold a lime avenue planted alongside the house's construction around 1720, the oldest of its kind in the city, but the oak stands apart from that formal design, a survivor from an entirely different era of the landscape's history rather than a planned garden feature. Bristol City Council now manages the estate's parkland, keeping it free and open to walkers, cyclists and anyone tracing the boundary between what Southwell built and what was already standing when he arrived.

trees.name: The Planes of Queen Square

location.address: Queen Square, Bristol BS1 4QS

trees.story: Bristol's city council built Queen Square between 1699 and 1720 on reclaimed marshland, selling plots to the city's merchants for grand townhouses around a formal green, one of the largest and earliest Georgian squares in England. The council planted 257 trees there in avenues as early as 1716, but almost none of that original planting survives. The double lines of London Planes that ring the square's edge today were planted later, probably in the 1880s, replacing whatever had come before. The square witnessed real violence in October 1831, when rioters protesting the House of Lords' rejection of electoral reform burned roughly a hundred buildings around its edges, including the Customs House and the Mansion House, in one of the most destructive urban riots in 19th-century Britain; the west side of the square was entirely rebuilt afterward. The planes now ringing the square postdate that fire by half a century, but they have had a century and a half since to grow into the mature canopy that shades the square's paths today, standing over a green that has been rebuilt, replanted and repurposed more than once since 1699.
verified_sources: https://bristoltreeforum.org/meet-bristols-remarkable-trees/veteran-trees-in-the-public-realm/ (Bristol Tree Forum survey: the largest London Plane in Queen Square, girth 510 cm; other planes there are smaller)
trees.access: Free, open access, public square
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Bristol Temple Meads railway station
trees.notes: Wikipedia's Queen Square, Bristol page and the Bristol Radical History Group's dedicated 1831 riot article corroborate the square's construction history (1699-1720), the 1716 original planting (257 trees, largely lost), the current planes dating to 'probably after 1882', and the 1831 riot's destruction and rebuilding of the west side. Bristol Tree Forum's survey independently lists a Queens Square plane at 510cm girth, 180 years, a slightly older estimate than the '1880s' planting date implies; age range widened to honestly straddle both figures rather than picking one. Presented as a single ensemble entry (the ringed double avenue) per the collectible-point test, not one tree standing in for the whole square. Photo: Wikimedia Commons file 'London Planes Queens Square - geograph.org.uk - 91527.jpg' (michael, CC BY-SA 2.0), geotagged directly at Queen Square, an unambiguous match for this ensemble entry. Viewed directly 2026-07-31 (a session with working image tooling): a row of mature plane trees fills the frame in a park setting, daylight, colour, clearly the ensemble described, approved.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the double row of London Planes ringing the edge of Queen Square, planted around the 1880s after the square's 1831 riot fire. They line the square's perimeter paths.

trees.name: The Strawberries and Cream Tree

location.address: Rodney Road, Backwell, North Somerset
location.neighbourhood: Backwell, North Somerset; day-trip distance from Bristol, about 9.5km

trees.story:
One trunk, two colours of blossom, and it is not two trees. A Kanzan flowering cherry was grafted onto wild cherry rootstock, and instead of one winning, tissue from both parents grew on together as a single tree. That makes it a graft chimera: pink Kanzan flowers along one side, white wild-cherry flowers along the other, open at the same time on the same trunk. It is one of only two cherry chimeras of this kind known in England, the other at Portchester in Hampshire.

Nobody knows who planted it. It went into council land on Rodney Road in the late 1950s, an ordinary-looking street tree that turned out to be a botanical accident worth travelling for, and the children of Backwell gave it the name that stuck. Every spring since, the village has watched one tree flower in two colours.

The last year has been hard on it. Council tree officers found it struggling after a long dry spell in 2025, and it now stands ringed by protective fencing keeping the traffic of an 800-home development off its roots, with mulching, a crown lift and deadwood removal scheduled. It is alive and being nursed rather than written off, and the fencing does not block the view.

It is free and on a public road, nine minutes by train from Bristol Temple Meads to Nailsea and Backwell, then a short walk. Come in April: outside blossom season the whole point of the tree is invisible.

best_time.label: April, when it opens pink and white blossom on the same trunk

trees.access: Free, on council-owned land beside a public road (Rodney Road, Backwell), visible and reachable at any time. Currently ringed by protective metal fencing to keep construction traffic for a nearby housing development away from its roots; the fencing does not block viewing.
trees.transport: Nailsea & Backwell railway station is about a 9-minute GWR train from Bristol Temple Meads (services roughly every 30 minutes), with Rodney Road a short walk from the station in Backwell village.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by pink blossom on one side of the crown and white on the other from a single trunk, currently ringed by protective metal fencing. It stands beside Rodney Road in Backwell.

trees.name: The Harbour Wall Fig

location.address: Floating Harbour wall east of Bristol Bridge, Castle Park, Bristol BS1

trees.story:
This fig does not grow in the ground. It grows out of the thirty-foot harbour wall just east of Bristol Bridge, a wall that was once part of Bristol Castle's defences, and how it got there, or when, the Bristol Tree Forum calls a mystery.

The likeliest answer is an accident of trade. A Bristol river blogger who follows the figs along the Avon, the harbour and the Malago believes they were seeded by fruit from boats and by ballast. The same blogger traced a huge fig opposite the old brewery through historic photographs from 1905, the 1920s, 1930 and 1951, and thinks it the oldest of at least two figs in Castle Park. This one grows in that spot. Neither source says in so many words that it is the same plant, so its century and more rests on those photographs and its position.

Every so often it is cut hard back to keep it clear of the river traffic. On 31 July 2018 a storm pulled half of it out of the wall, and the Harbour Master's team cleared the wreckage from the water. What grows there now is the regrowth, smaller than the mass in the old photographs, and still alive: people recorded it there in July and again in October 2026.

It is a wall tree, so nobody has measured a trunk. If you know when it first appeared, tell us.
trees.access: Free. Seen from the Castle Park path along the Floating Harbour, open at all times at no charge (Bristol City Council). The tree grows out of the harbour wall itself, so it is viewed from the path, not reached.
trees.transport: Beside Bristol Bridge, about 0.55 km (7 min walk) from Queen Square and about 1 km (13 min walk) from Bristol Temple Meads.
trees.notes: Source A, Bristol Tree Forum (ST 5910 7303, converts to 51.45476,-2.59002): a huge fig in the thirty-foot vertical wall of Bristol Docks just east of Bristol Bridge; the wall was part of the old castle's defences; how it got established and how long ago is a mystery; 'every so often it is heavily reduced so that it does not create problems for the river traffic'. Source B, Avon Stories (a Bristol river blogger, Sept 2018): at least two figs in Castle Park; the huge one opposite the old brewery is thought the oldest, visible in historic photographs from 1905 (Know Your Place), the 1920s, 1930 and 1951; figs along the Avon, harbour and Malago were seeded by accident from trade (fruit from boats, ballast). A storm on 31 July 2018 pulled half of it out of the wall and the Harbour Master team removed the debris from the water. Alive now: two iNaturalist observations of Ficus carica with GPS accuracy 3 to 4 m at 51.45485,-2.58990 (2026-07-23, research grade; 2026-10-14), which is within about 10 m of the BTF grid reference; confirmed pin on that evidence (a GPS fix at the tree). Caveat for the writer: after the 2018 storm the tree is a regrown, reduced fig, not the full mass that stood in 1905; whether the two sources' 'huge' fig is exactly this plant is inferred from the position, not stated. Age: no source dates this specimen; 'over a century' rests only on the blogger saying the fig is visible in 1905 photographs, so state that as the blogger's claim. No girth (a wall tree). Lead, not delivered: the second sprawling fig on the New Cut bank by the Bath Bridge roundabout (BTF, ST 5961 7215, no GPS or recent observation found).

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it grows, out of the vertical harbour wall itself rather than from the ground. It stands just east of Bristol Bridge, seen from the Castle Park path along the water.

trees.name: The Royal Fort Black Mulberry

location.address: Royal Fort Gardens, Tyndall Avenue, Bristol BS8 1UH

trees.story:
The largest black mulberry in Bristol is 2.3 metres round, and it grows in a university garden that anyone can walk into. The Bristol Tree Forum, which listed the city's biggest trees species by species, gives it the title. The University of Bristol keeps Royal Fort Gardens open to the public every day of the year, with no ticket.

Mulberries are not known for standing up straight. The Forum notes they are often found growing horizontally, and this one leans. A mulberry register from 2007 put a tree near the east exit by the engineering building, overhanging a path, which is a rough guide to where to look rather than a promise.

What nobody has written down is its age. There is no planting record and no estimate, nothing that dates the trunk at all. If you know when it went in, or have an old photograph of the garden with it in, tell us.

What is on record is that it lives. Visitors logged it on iNaturalist in April 2019 and again in July 2025, each time within a few metres of the spot the Forum's survey gives, which is how the map knows where it stands.

It sits below Tyndall Avenue and the Wills Memorial Building, a few minutes up Park Street from College Green, so it fits easily into a walk between Queen Square and Clifton. Come in July or August, when the dark fruit ripens and stains the ground beneath.

best_time.label: July and August, when the dark fruit ripens and stains the ground beneath

trees.access: Free. The University of Bristol opens Royal Fort Gardens to the public daily all year, with no ticket (its other gardens are by invitation or tour).
trees.transport: Below Tyndall Avenue and the Wills Memorial Building, about 0.9 km (12 min walk) north-west of Queen Square, a few minutes up Park Street from College Green.
trees.notes: FLAGGED: one survey plus GPS observations; no age. Bristol Tree Forum (ST 5833 7331, converts to 51.45722,-2.60114): 'the largest' Black Mulberry in the city, in the gardens of the Royal Fort, girth 230 cm; mulberries are often found growing horizontally. A Garden News UK column (2021) calls an old, bent mulberry its favourite thing in the gardens (read as a search snippet only; not used for a figure). Pin: three iNaturalist observations of Morus nigra at Royal Fort Gardens (2019-04-26, 2019-04-27, 2025-07-22, GPS accuracy 4 to 8 m, research grade for two) sit at 51.45723 to 51.45727,-2.60116 to -2.60126, within about 7 m of the BTF grid reference, so the tree is placed and confirmed; the 2025 observation also shows it alive. A mulberry register entry (2007) puts one 'near the east exit by the engineering building overhanging a path', a coarse hint only. Royal Fort Gardens is a walk-through garden, not a small site, so no location_site. BTF also names a young Dawyck beech, Italian cypress, Kapuka and young Yellow Buckeye in the same garden, and a Persian Ironwood by the Wills Tower (ST5815 7318); all minor, not delivered. No sentence available that dates the mulberry; if the writer wants to say it is old, only the 230 cm girth and the leaning habit are sourced.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the lean: a black mulberry 2.3 metres round, growing sideways rather than upright. It stands in Royal Fort Gardens, towards the east exit by the engineering building.

trees.name: The Brandon Hill Oak

location.address: Brandon Hill, Bristol BS1 5RR (near the park-keepers' compound)

trees.story:
The oldest tree on Brandon Hill grows in the one corner of the park the public is not meant to wander into. The Bristol Tree Forum places this oak just inside the park keepers' compound, and adds that it dominates the area all the same. Its boughs reach about twenty metres.

The trunk is five metres round. The Forum puts the tree at around 300 years, its own estimate from the survey rather than a dated record, so read it as somewhere between 200 and 400. The Forum also calls Brandon Hill an extraordinary park that has been public open space for 800 years, and this oak the oldest tree on it.

Here is what we cannot tell you. Whether the trunk stands in plain view from the park paths, or behind a depot fence with only the crown reaching over, is not something any source we found settles. A crown that size should be hard to miss from the paths around the compound, but nobody has confirmed the view. The pin comes from the survey's grid reference and is approximate.

The hill rises right behind College Green and the top of Park Street, about thirteen minutes' walk from Queen Square, so it is an easy detour on the way to Clifton. If you have stood there, tell us which side of the fence the trunk is on and where the best view is. One sentence from someone who has looked would settle what three sources could not.
trees.access: Free. Brandon Hill is a Bristol City Council public park. The Bristol Tree Forum places the oak just inside the park keepers' compound, so it may stand behind a depot fence: see it from the park paths. Whether the trunk is in view from outside the compound is not confirmed.
trees.transport: Beside College Green and Park Street, about 1 km (13 min walk) west of Queen Square.
trees.notes: FLAGGED, single source for the tree itself. Bristol Tree Forum veteran survey (ST 5781 7291, converts to 51.45359,-2.60857): Common Oak, girth 500 cm, 'age 300' (BTF's estimate), 'magnificent tree with boughs twenty metres long', 'just inside the park-keepers compound but dominates the area', 'the oldest tree in this extraordinary park, which has been a public open space for 800 years' (the 800 years is BTF's phrase; the council and Parks and Gardens UK page confirm Brandon Hill is a public park, the council page lists a tree trail by the Friends of Brandon Hill, which I could not read as it is a compressed PDF). Alive: lifecheck.py returned RECENT 2024-12-01 (iNaturalist, generic nearby observation); no observation of a large oak at this exact point found, three oak observations lie 80 to 120 m away. Access question to settle on the ground: whether the oak is visible from outside the compound. Walking cluster note: the Wellingtonia (girth 300 cm, planted 1973, BTF ST5787 7286) and the Keaki, Swedish whitebeam and Pride of India on this hill are young or small and were not delivered.
trees.pin_source: Bristol Tree Forum veteran survey grid reference ST 5781 7291 (converted, approximate)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the boughs, about twenty metres long, on an oak five metres round. It stands on Brandon Hill just inside the park keepers' compound, so look from the paths around it.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon in Victoria Square

location.address: Victoria Square, Clifton, Bristol BS8 4ES

trees.story:
Before the war, you needed a key to stand under this cedar. Victoria Square in Clifton was a residents' garden behind four locked gates, and only keyholders got in. Then its railings were taken away in wartime, the garden was left open to everyone, and it has stayed that way. Bristol City Council now looks after it as a public park.

The cedar is the reason to come. Its trunk is 5.95 metres round and its branches run out horizontally for about twenty metres. The Bristol Tree Forum counts it among the few trees left from the square's original planting and estimates its age at 150 years. When that planting happened is less settled. The Clifton and Hotwells Improvement Society dates the square to about 1840, another source to about 1860, and no source ties the cedar to either year, so somewhere between 150 and 190 years is the honest answer.

A memoir published by the same society remembers a large stone urn standing beneath the cedar. The urn is gone, and so is much of the old planting. The garden was cleared and replanted in 2015, and the cedar stayed.

It keeps old company. A fern-leaved beech nearby, 4.8 metres round, also belongs to the original planting by the Forum's account, and the square holds an old black mulberry growing sideways, an Italian maple and a chimera hornbeam besides. Twenty minutes' walk west of Queen Square, it is where a walk through central Bristol's old trees ends.
trees.access: Free. Victoria Square garden is a council-maintained public park (it was a keyholders' garden until the wartime removal of its railings), open to walk through.
trees.transport: Central Clifton, about 1.6 km (20 min walk) west of Queen Square and about 10 min walk up from College Green and Park Street.
trees.notes: Source A, Bristol Tree Forum veteran survey (Richard Bland, ST 5728 7313, which converts to 51.45553,-2.61623, inside the square): girth 595 cm, 'age 150 years', 'one of the few trees from the original planting', horizontal branches about 20 m long. BTF's age is its own estimate, so the range here is broad (BTF says 150; the Clifton and Hotwells society dates the square's first planting to about 1840, and another source gives about 1860; no source says this tree belongs to a dated planting, so no bridge made). Source B, Clifton and Hotwells Improvement Society's communal-gardens guide: Victoria Square (ca. 1840) is now a public park, the Council maintains it, and a fine Lebanon cedar is among the surviving original plantings; a 2015 clearance and replanting is recorded. Source C, Dick Isles memoir (same society): a large stone urn once stood under the cedar of Lebanon; before the war the gardens had four locked gates and residents held keys; wartime railing removal left them open to all. Alive: lifecheck.py 51.4562 -2.6163 returned RECENT 2026-05-17 (iNaturalist, generic nearby observation, not proof for this trunk); the square was replanted 2015 and the cedar is described as surviving. Same spot, other trees to fold into the page as context only: Fern-leaved Beech (BTF, girth 480 cm, original planting c1860, ST5727 7310), an old horizontal Black Mulberry, an Italian Maple (girth 280 cm), and a chimera hornbeam; none is a separate collectible point. Pin is the BTF grid reference (10 m resolution, judged unreliable by an earlier pass), so approximate; the square is small and the cedar is the dominant tree. Hard-rule check: this is not one of the private Clifton garden squares the earlier pass left out; the Clifton society and council sources say Victoria Square specifically is now public. Single-species survey plus two local-society pages; not a register.
trees.pin_source: Bristol Tree Forum veteran survey grid reference ST 5728 7313 (converted; approximate, inside the square)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its branches, running out horizontally for about twenty metres from a trunk 5.95 metres round. It is the largest tree in Victoria Square garden, bigger than the fern-leaved beech nearby.

trees.name: The Mina Road Park Plane

location.address: Mina Road Park, St Werburghs, Bristol BS2 9YG

trees.story:
Of all the Bristol trees the Bristol Tree Forum has measured at more than five metres round, this plane comes thirteenth. It stands in Mina Road Park in St Werburghs, 6.2 metres round, the largest of a group of London planes that the Forum says were all planted at the same time, around 1880.

That date makes them a small puzzle. The park itself opened on 30 June 1886, laid out by Frederick Ashmead with a Victorian scheme of Wellingtonia, deodar and Cryptomeria, on ground given to the Corporation in 1884. If the Forum is right, the planes were growing here before the park was a park, and no source we found explains why. Wikipedia's account of the park mentions an older group of London planes alongside its acacias and Norway maples, but gives them no date. A planting around 1880 is plausible. It is not proven, and both the girth and the year are the Forum's own figures, so the age here runs from 120 to 160 years.

The Forum also does not say which trunk in the group is the big one, and all the planes are the same age. The pin is approximate, from the survey's grid reference. Look for the widest trunk among the planes; at 6.2 metres it should stand out.

It is a 35-minute walk north-east of Queen Square, near Stapleton Road and Montpelier stations. If you know why these planes are older than the park around them, tell us.
trees.access: Free. Mina Road Park is a Bristol City Council park, open all year.
trees.transport: St Werburghs, about 2.6 km (35 min walk) north-east of Queen Square, near Stapleton Road and Montpelier stations.
trees.notes: FLAGGED, single source for the tree. Bristol Tree Forum (ST 6014 7443, converts to 51.46743,-2.57521): the group of plane trees in Mina Road Park are 'stunning' and 'all the same age, having been planted c 1880'; this one is the largest, girth 620 cm (the 13th largest tree in BTF's over-5-metre list). Age is BTF's planting date, so about 140 years, not independently checked: Wikipedia says the park was laid out by Frederick Ashmead and opened 30 June 1886 with a Victorian planting scheme of Wellingtonia, deodar and Cryptomeria, and that the present-day park has an older group of London planes alongside acacia and Norway maples but gives no ages; Parks and Gardens UK says the ground was given to the Corporation in 1884. So a c1880 planting predating the 1886 opening is plausible but unconfirmed. Alive: lifecheck returned RECENT 2024-02-12 (iNaturalist, generic nearby observation, no plane-specific record). The 620 cm girth is large for a plane of that age; a writer should state it as BTF's measurement. Outside the walkable centre cluster (about 2.6 km from Queen Square). Cluster note: the BTF entry says all the planes are the same age, so which trunk is the 620 cm one cannot be told from sources.
trees.pin_source: Bristol Tree Forum veteran survey grid reference ST 6014 7443 (converted, approximate)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the widest of the group of London planes in Mina Road Park, 6.2 metres round; the other planes there are the same age but smaller.

trees.name: The Saville Road Horse Chestnut

location.address: Saville Road, Durdham Down (the Downs), Bristol BS9

trees.story:
The largest horse chestnut on the Downs has bleeding canker, and when the Bristol Tree Forum last looked, it was carrying on regardless. The Forum's survey calls it diseased but still vigorous, with a trunk five metres round, and estimates it at about 200 years old. That is an estimate from the survey and nothing firmer, so read it as somewhere between 150 and 250.

It stands beside Saville Road on the edge of Durdham Down, the open common in the north of the city that the Downs Committee manages for the public. The Forum thinks the line of chestnuts along Westbury Park Road was probably planted at the same time, and notes that a number of other trees have succumbed in the past few years and had to be felled.

Which is why this page comes with a warning. The Forum's survey carries no date. Its list goes back to 2016, with comments running to 2023, and we have found no recent photograph of this trunk. It may still be standing, diseased and vigorous as described. It may have gone the way of the trees around it. The pin, from the survey's grid reference, is approximate.

If you walk past Saville Road, tell us which it is, and send a photograph if the tree still stands.

If it is, come in May, when the white candles stand upright over the crown.

best_time.label: May, when white candles stand upright over the whole crown

trees.access: Free. The Downs are public open common managed by the Downs Committee; the tree stands beside Saville Road on the edge of Durdham Down, open at all times. Not confirmed standing since the Bristol Tree Forum's undated survey.
trees.transport: About 3.2 km (40 min walk) north of Queen Square on the edge of Durdham Down; city buses serve the Downs.
trees.notes: FLAGGED, single source, undated. Bristol Tree Forum (ST 5712 7574, converts to 51.47898,-2.61885): the largest horse chestnut on the Downs, girth 500 cm, age 200 (BTF estimate), 'diseased with bleeding canker, but remains vigorous'; the line along Westbury Park Road was probably planted at the same time; 'a number of other trees have succumbed in the past few years and had to be felled'. The BTF page has no survey date (the forum's list dates from 2016, with a comment thread to 2023), so the tree may have been felled since: lifecheck returned RECENT 2026-04-08 but it is a generic nearby observation. Alive status needs a recent photo of this trunk before the page promises it. Not in the central walk (3 km out). Dropped as the more central choice if the writer prefers: nothing else on the Downs has a source and an exact place.
trees.pin_source: Bristol Tree Forum veteran survey grid reference ST 5712 7574 (converted, approximate)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, five metres round, the largest horse chestnut on the Downs. It stands beside Saville Road on the edge of Durdham Down.

trees.name: The Parish Yew, Leigh Woods

location.address: Parish wall, Leigh Woods National Nature Reserve, near the National Trust reserve office, Valley Road, Bristol BS8 3PL

official_register.name: Ancient Yew Group database, Leigh Woods (1)

trees.access: Free. Leigh Woods is open woodland run by the National Trust; the veteran tree walk (1 mile, 30 to 45 minutes, easy) starts at the North Road entrance, grid ref ST555730; roadside parking on North Road.
trees.transport: Bus 357, 358 or 359 along the A369, nearest stop about 100 m from North Road, then about 10 minutes on foot to the tree. Clifton Down station 2.6 km.

location_site.name: Parish wall by the NT reserve office, Leigh Woods

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk bulging around the stones of the old parish wall, with stretches of wall removed either side and woodchip over the roots. It stands beside the surfaced path near the reserve office.
trees.story:
This yew is slowly eating a wall. It grows in a gap in the old stone parish boundary that runs through Leigh Woods, and its trunk has bulged out around the stones and swallowed part of them. The National Trust, which looks after the woods, eventually stopped arguing with it. It took away short stretches of wall on either side to give the tree room, and laid woodchip around its roots.

The Trust puts it at approximately 500 years old and calls it one of the oldest trees in Leigh Woods. That is the Trust's estimate rather than a ring count. The Ancient Yew Group, which keeps a database of Britain's old yews, measured the trunk at 4.6 metres round in 2004 and classes it as ancient, without offering an age of its own.

It is also what foresters call a maiden tree. Many old trees in working woods were pollarded or coppiced, cut back so they would regrow as a crop of poles. The Trust says this one never was. Whatever happened to the wood around it, the yew has been left to grow in its own shape for its whole life.

A parish wall is built to mark a line for good. Here the wall is the thing that had to give way. The tree is stage 2 of the Trust's veteran tree walk, about ten minutes from the North Road entrance.

trees.name: The Nightingale Valley Plane

location.address: Nightingale Valley, beside Brislington Brook and its weir, Brislington, Bristol

trees.access: Free. Public woodland path along Brislington Brook (Nightingale Valley); the trunk can be seen from the path by the weir. Paths can be muddy; no hours.
trees.transport: Bristol Temple Meads about 4 km; nearest rail stop St Anne's Park about 600 m north-west by the brook path (computed from coordinates, not checked on a timetable).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bricked-up opening in its vast hollow trunk, 6.75 metres round. It stands beside the weir on Brislington Brook in Nightingale Valley, seen from the woodland path.
trees.story:
Somebody bricked this tree up. The London plane beside the weir in Nightingale Valley is hollow, and people had taken to lighting fires inside it, so the open trunk was filled in with brickwork to stop them. It worked. The plane is still alive, and the brick patch has become the easiest way to tell it from everything else along Brislington Brook.

It is a big tree to have survived that. The Bristol Tree Forum measured the trunk at 6.75 metres round, says the crown fills the little valley of the brook, and estimates it at about 250 years old. That age is the Forum's own estimate from the size, not a planting date. The Forum also thinks the tree was probably associated with nearby Brislington House, though it gives no record of who planted it or when.

A walker who wrote up the brook path in 2018 passed on the local view that this is the oldest plane in Bristol. Nobody has published the measurements to settle it, so take that as what people round here say rather than a fact we can stand behind. It would not be a surprising title. The other big planes the city is known for, in Queen Square and Mina Road Park, were planted around the 1880s.

The brook path can be muddy after rain. The whole trunk can be seen from the path by the weir, with no need to leave it.

trees.name: The Monterey Cypress at Bishops Knoll

location.address: Bishops Knoll Wood, Bramble Lane, Stoke Bishop, Bristol BS9 1JH

trees.access: Free. Woodland Trust wood, open access; main entrance on Bramble Lane (public road with pavement, wide gate). A public footpath crosses the site; some uneven steps. No car park, a few spaces on Bramble Lane.
trees.transport: Nearest bus stop Julian Road, 1 km walk on pavement (Woodland Trust).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the Victorian iron railings still standing round its trunk, which is over seven metres in girth. It stands inside Bishops Knoll Wood, among the old grounds of the demolished Knoll mansion.
trees.story:
The house whose garden this cypress grew up in has been gone for half a century, and its railings have not. Bishops Knoll Wood was once the grounds of The Knoll, a mansion built in the late 19th century for Peter Prankerd and demolished in the 1970s. The Monterey cypress still stands inside the Victorian ironwork that was put round it, a fence guarding a garden that no longer exists.

It has grown into what the Bristol Tree Forum calls a colossal specimen. The Forum measured the trunk at 7.1 metres round, and the Woodland Trust, which now owns the wood, gives it a girth of over seven metres.

The Forum's age is a piece of reasoning rather than a record. Monterey cypress reached Britain in 1839, and the Forum argues this one cannot have gone in earlier than 1860, which puts it somewhere around 150 to 170 years old. Nobody has a planting date.

The species has a second claim on British gardens. The Forum points out that Monterey cypress is one parent of the Leyland cypress, the fast-growing conifer behind so many garden hedges. This is what one side of that family looks like when it is left alone for a century and a half.

The wood is free to walk into from Bramble Lane. A giant coast redwood and a vast Austrian black pine stand in the same old grounds.

trees.name: The Bundle-planted Sessile Oak, Bishops Knoll

location.address: Bishops Knoll Wood, Bramble Lane entrance, Stoke Bishop, Bristol BS9 1JH

trees.access: Free. Woodland Trust wood, open access, entrance on Bramble Lane; the oak is the first big tree on entering (Woodland Trust).
trees.transport: Nearest bus stop Julian Road, 1 km walk on pavement (Woodland Trust).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the several fused stems that make one broad trunk, seven metres round. It stands close to the Bramble Lane entrance among apple and other fruit trees, partly screened by young ash.
trees.story:
This oak may be six trees pretending to be one. The Woodland Trust thinks it was planted as a bundle, six or so young oaks set in a single hole, which over the centuries fused into one trunk. That would explain why it is so portly, seven metres round. The Bristol Tree Forum agrees it may have been a bundle planting, noting that its several stems do not appear to grow from an old pollard cut, the other usual reason an oak ends up with many trunks.

How old it is depends on whom you ask. The Woodland Trust, which owns the wood, says it could be as much as 600 years old and probably dates from the medieval deer park that once covered this ground. The Forum puts it at 700. Both are estimates from the size of a tree whose size may be the work of six. Either way it was growing here centuries before The Knoll, the Victorian mansion whose grounds became this wood, and long before the Monterey cypress a short walk away.

The two sources also disagree on how easy it is to spot. The Trust describes it looming through apple and other fruit trees as the first thing to catch the eye when you come in from Bramble Lane. The Forum says it is disguised by young ash trees and not easy to find. Look near the entrance, among the fruit trees, for a broad oak made of several fused stems.

trees.name: The Blaise Meadow Sweet Chestnut

location.address: Meadow off Henbury Road, Blaise Castle Estate, Henbury, Bristol BS10 7QS

trees.access: Free. Blaise Castle Estate is a council-owned public park (Wikipedia); meadow off Henbury Road. No opening hours found.
trees.transport: Bus to Henbury / Blaise Castle area; not checked. About 7 km north-west of the centre (computed).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the vast horizontal limbs spreading from a trunk seven metres round. It stands in the meadow off Henbury Road on the Blaise Castle Estate, beside a sycamore that grows on five trunks.
trees.story:
If the Bristol Tree Forum's estimate is right, this chestnut was already around 300 years old when Humphry Repton came to Blaise to design the parkland. The Forum puts it at about 550 years, with a trunk seven metres round, and describes its vast horizontal branches reaching out across the meadow off Henbury Road.

That age is the Forum's own figure, worked out from a tree nobody has dated, and we have found no second written source for this particular chestnut. A girth of seven metres is in keeping with a sweet chestnut several centuries old, but treat 550 as an estimate. On the Forum's figure it would have been growing here through the late medieval centuries, the Civil War, and the years after 1789, when the banker John Scandrett Harford bought the estate and had Repton reshape the grounds into the Picturesque park that is now free for anyone to walk.

The chestnut does not have the meadow to itself, and its neighbours are part of the reason to come. The Forum lists a sycamore beside it that grows on five trunks, each about 2.8 metres round and seven metres around all together, and the stump of an old common lime that has rotted down and thrown up a thicket of thin new trunks from its base. Three trees in one field, each refusing to grow the way a tree in a textbook does.

If you know more about its history, tell us.

trees.name: The Wellingtonias by the Lower Pond, Combe Dingle

location.address: Combe Dingle, by the lower pond on the Trym, Blaise Castle Estate, Bristol BS10

trees.access: Free. Within the public Blaise Castle Estate (council-owned, Wikipedia); on the slope beside the stream near the lower pond.
trees.transport: Not checked; Coombe Dingle suburb adjoins the estate. About 6.5 km north-west of the centre (computed).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as two very tall giant sequoias standing together, the thicker one, 7.1 metres round, on the stream side. They stand on the slope beside the stream near the lower pond in Combe Dingle.
trees.story:
Two Californian giants stand thirty metres apart at the bottom of a Bristol valley, beside a stream and a small pond. The thicker of the pair measures 7.1 metres round, which makes it, according to the Bristol Tree Forum, the largest of the three Wellingtonias on the Blaise Castle Estate. Its partner, about 30 metres away, is 6 metres round.

Wellingtonia is the British name for the giant sequoia, the species of the biggest trees on Earth in the Sierra Nevada, and in Britain it is a newcomer. The Forum's account is that seed reached the Veitch nursery in 1855. It dates the smaller of these two at about 150 years. That is an estimate from the species' arrival, not a planting record, so the pair are best thought of as somewhere between 150 and 170 years old.

That makes them young by the standards of this list, and by the standards of their own species, which can live for thousands of years in California. Here, beside the lower pond on the Trym, they are a century and a half into that. The third of the estate's Wellingtonias, 33 metres tall, stands near the house, about 900 metres away.

We have only the Forum's survey for these trees. If you know more about who planted them, tell us.

trees.name: The Oldbury Court Sweet Chestnut

location.address: Oldbury Court Estate, Fishponds, Bristol BS16

trees.access: Free. Oldbury Court Estate is a public park beside the River Frome (Wikipedia).
trees.transport: Fishponds, about 4.8 km north-east of the centre (Wikipedia); bus not checked.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing alone in the middle of a wide grassy area, a clean trunk 5.9 metres round under a broad head of branches. It stands in the open centre of Oldbury Court Estate.
trees.story:
One tree runs this park. The Bristol Tree Forum says this sweet chestnut dominates Oldbury Court, a massive veteran standing on its own in the middle of a wide stretch of grass, with a clean trunk 5.9 metres round and a fine head of branches above it. In a park of big trees, it is the one you see first.

The Forum estimates it at about 400 years old. That is the Forum's figure, from a tree that has never been dated, and we have only its survey for this particular chestnut, so take the number as a careful guess rather than a record. On that estimate it would have been growing here since the early 1600s, long before Oldbury Court became a public park in Fishponds and before Humphry Repton, the landscape designer, was brought in to advise on the grounds.

Sweet chestnuts are not native to Britain. Nobody has left a record of how this one came to stand here. Its neighbours give a sense of the place. The Forum also lists two big oaks on the northern edge of the estate, above the gorge of the River Frome, at around 380 years old.

If you know its history, tell us.

trees.name: The Hermitage Wood Horse Chestnuts, Stoke Park

location.address: Hermitage Wood, Stoke Park, Stoke Gifford / Bristol BS16

trees.access: Free. Hermitage Wood lies in Stoke Park, a public park; BTF does not state hours. Access not independently checked.
trees.transport: Not checked; Stoke Park is about 5 km north-east of the centre (computed).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the biggest of three old horse chestnuts, 5.5 metres round, the largest trees in Hermitage Wood. It stands on the eastern edge of the wood in Stoke Park.
trees.story:
The biggest trees in Hermitage Wood are not the native oaks or ash you might expect, but three horse chestnuts, a species from the Balkans. The Bristol Tree Forum records all three as veterans. The largest, on the eastern edge of the wood, is 5.5 metres round. The other two, 5.05 and 5 metres, stand in a corner of the wood and on the northern edge of the main path, all within about 300 metres of each other.

The Forum thinks they were probably planted for aesthetic reasons, and that they are probably about 300 years old. That age is the Forum's guess, and we could not find a second source to confirm it. If it holds, they would be old for their kind, a species that only reached Britain in the 17th century.

The wood sits inside Stoke Park, a public park on the north-eastern edge of Bristol. Nobody has published who planted them, or exactly when.

They are at their best in May, when the big leaves are fresh and the trees carry their upright spikes of white flowers, and again in autumn when the conkers come down. If you know more about the trio, tell us.

best_time.label: May, when all three chestnuts carry their upright spikes of white flowers

trees.name: The Kings Weston Deodar

location.address: Beside Kings Weston House, Kings Weston Lane, Bristol BS11 0UT

trees.access: Free to see from the parkland around the house (the Kings Weston estate parkland is open; the house itself is a conference and wedding venue). Opening hours not stated.
trees.transport: Not checked; Kings Weston is about 7 km north-west of the centre (computed).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the huge limb that leaves the trunk almost at ground level and runs out sideways. It stands beside Kings Weston House, a deodar cedar 4.3 metres round.
trees.story:
Most cedars hold their great limbs well above your head. This one throws a huge branch out sideways almost at ground level, from so low on the trunk that the limb starts where most trees are still all trunk. The Bristol Tree Forum picked it as one of twenty remarkable Bristol trees that hold no national record, and that branch is the reason.

The tree is a deodar, the Himalayan cedar, with a trunk 4.3 metres round, and it grows right beside Kings Weston House. Sir John Vanbrugh designed it for Edward Southwell in the early 18th century, and it was remodelled between 1845 and 1850. Whether the cedar is as old as that remodelling, no source we have found says, and the Forum gives no age. So it stays undated here, and if you know when it was planted, tell us.

The parkland around the house is open to walk through, and the cedar can be seen from it. The house itself is a wedding and conference venue rather than a museum. The Oak of Kings Weston, older than Vanbrugh's house, stands in the same estate and makes the pair worth one walk.

trees.name: The Snuff Mills Quarry-edge Oak

location.address: Edge of the former quarry cliff, Snuff Mills park, Frome Valley, Bristol BS16

trees.access: Free. Snuff Mills is a public riverside park on the Frome (Wikipedia). The tree is on the edge of the path above the quarry cliff, and seen from the lower path in winter.
trees.transport: Not checked; Stapleton, about 5 km north-east of the centre (computed).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its position, a squat old oak right on the lip of the old quarry cliff at the edge of the upper path. In winter it shows from the lower path by the river.
trees.story:
This oak grows on the lip of a sheer drop. Snuff Mills was quarried once, and the old quarry face along the Frome valley is now a vertical cliff. The oak stands right at its top edge, beside the path, with nothing much between its roots and the air. The Bristol Tree Forum, which put it on its list of twenty remarkable Bristol trees that hold no national record, says simply that it defies gravity.

The Forum calls it very ancient and squat, which is about all anyone has written down. There is no published girth and no age, not even a rough estimate, and we have found no second source for this particular tree. If you know how old it is, or have measured it, tell us.

What the Forum does say is where to look. In summer the oak is one tree among many along the top path. In winter, with the leaves down, it shows from the lower path along the river, a low, broad shape hunched on the very edge of the cliff above you. That is the view worth coming for, and it needs no scrambling.

Snuff Mills is a public riverside park on the Frome in Stapleton, free and open to walk. A small-leaved lime with weeping branches grows on the riverbank a few hundred metres along the river, listed by the same survey.

best_time.label: winter, when the bare oak shows from the lower path, hunched on the edge of the quarry cliff
